# Setup

```{r}
options(conflicts.policy = "depends.ok")
library(tidyverse)
plot_grid <- cowplot::plot_grid
source("https://github.com/jjcurtin/lab_support/blob/main/format_path.R?raw=true")
source("https://github.com/jjcurtin/lab_support/blob/main/fun_eda.R?raw=true")
source("https://github.com/jjcurtin/lab_support/blob/main/fun_plots.R?raw=true")
source("https://github.com/jjcurtin/study_llmpanel/blob/main/scripts/functions_llmpanel.R?raw=true")
library(tidymodels)

path_processed <- format_path("llmpanel/data_processed")

# Read in full panel
panel <- read_csv(here::here(path_processed, "panel.csv"),
                       show_col_types = FALSE)
```

# Constant Demographic Features

The following features will be used in all recipes, without changes across model configurations:

## Sex

Sex at birth will be used as a dummy coded, dichotomous predictor: female (0.5) or male (-0.5).

```{r}
panel |> count(dem_sex)

panel <- panel |> 
  mutate(dem_sex = if_else(dem_sex == "female", 0.5, -0.5))

panel |> count(dem_sex)
```

## Orientation

Sexual Orientation will be used with collapsed categories Straight/Other, resulting from a lack of variability for non-straight orientations within the sample. 

```{r}
panel |> count(dem_orientation)

panel <- panel |> 
  mutate(dem_orientation = if_else(dem_orientation == "straight", "straight", "other"))
       
panel |> count(dem_orientation)
```

## Race / Ethnicity

Race will be used with collapsed categories White Only/Other, resulting from a lack of variability for non-white ethnicity groups within the sample.

```{r}
panel <- panel |>
  mutate(
    white = !is.na(dem_race_white),
    other =
      !is.na(dem_race_native_alaskan) |
      !is.na(dem_race_asian) |
      !is.na(dem_race_hispanic) |
      !is.na(dem_race_black),
    dem_race = if_else(white & !other, -0.5, +0.5))

panel |> count(dem_race)
```

## Household Size

Household size will be used in its raw numeric form (`dem_n_household`).

```{r}
panel |> count(dem_n_household)
```

# Adjustable Demographic Features

## Age

Age can be used in its raw numeric predictor form, or it can be binned into roughly equal categories:

```{r}
panel <- panel |>
  mutate(dem_age_binned = cut(
    dem_age, breaks = c(18, 29, 39, 49, 59, Inf),
    labels = c("18-29", "30-39", "40-49", "50-59", "60+"),
    right = TRUE, include.lowest = TRUE))

panel |> count(dem_age_binned)
```

The binned age predictor can be treated as either an ordinal or just a multi-category variable.

## Education

Education will be handled in two possible ways: The first option will be to treat it as an ordinal predictor with increasing amounts of education, and other will be to collapse into 3 categories.

```{r}
panel <- panel |>
  mutate(dem_edu_collapsed = case_when(
    dem_education %in% c("high_school_or_ged", "less_than_high_school_or_ged_degree") ~ "High School or Less",
    dem_education == "some_college" ~ "Some College",
    dem_education %in% c("2_year_degree", "4_year_degree", "advanced_degree") ~ "2-Year Degree or Higher"
  ))

panel |> count(dem_edu_collapsed)
```

## Income (+ Household Adjusted)

Income will be handled in 3 possible ways: First will be to treat income bracket as either a multi-category or ordinal variable.

Another engineered feature will be 'Household Size-Adjusted Income':

```{r}
panel <- panel |>
  mutate(
    income_numeric = case_when(
      dem_income == "Less than $25,000"   ~ 12500, # Midpoint estimates for each bracket
      dem_income == "$25,000 - $37,499"   ~ 31250,
      dem_income == "$37,500 - $49,999"   ~ 43750,
      dem_income == "$50,000 - $74,999"   ~ 62500,
      dem_income == "$75,000 - $99,999"   ~ 87500,
      dem_income == "$100,000 - $149,999" ~ 125000,
      dem_income == "$150,000 - $199,999" ~ 175000,
      dem_income == "$200,000 or more"    ~ 250000 # The cap for this one is debatable
    ),
    dem_income_adjusted = income_numeric / sqrt(dem_n_household))
```

There is precedent for this feature, and logically it is used to reflect 'economies of scale' in a household environment. The cost of living when moving from a 1 -> 2 person household will be greater than moving from a 5 -> 6 person household is the primary assumption that justifies the transformation of household size. The most tenuous assumption of this feature is choosing a numeric estimate for our highest income bracket, which did not have a fixed cap.

Household size is a constant feature, so it is included in every recipe. When this feature is included in a recipe, it may or may not have a separate predictor for income bracket included. As in, this feature could be used in addition to income bracket, or as a replacement for it to reduce dimensionality.

## Interactions

When explicitly defining interactions is required, the following combinations will be considered:

- Age x Income x Education

- Sex x Race x Orientation

- Age x Household Size

- Income x Household Size

# Pivot Long Format

The pivot happens after all demographic features are engineered so they carry through to the message-level data. Note that the feature engineering chunks above modify `panel` in place and are not idempotent (e.g., re-running the sex recode sets everyone to -0.5), so re-run from the Setup chunk if needed.

```{r}
panel_long <- panel |>
  select(subid, dem_age:dem_minority,
         dem_race, dem_age_binned, dem_edu_collapsed,
         dem_income_adjusted,
         q1_legitimizing_1:q6_formality_1,
         `x1_hi_1_fl_1`:`x4_li_10_in_1`,
         -contains("timing"), -contains("attention")) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols= `x1_hi_1_fl_1`:`x4_li_10_in_1`,
    values_to = "message_rating",
    names_to = "message_type") |>
  separate(message_type,
           sep = "_", into = c(
             "survey_version", "context", "q_num", "tone_style"),
           extra = "drop") |> 
  mutate(
    style = if_else(substr(tone_style, 1, 1) == "f", "formal", "informal"),
    tone = case_when(
      substr(tone_style, 2, 2) == "l" ~ "legitimizing",
      substr(tone_style, 2, 2) == "n" ~ "norms",
      substr(tone_style, 2, 2) == "s" ~ "self_efficacy",
      substr(tone_style, 2, 2) == "a" ~ "acknowledging",
      substr(tone_style, 2, 2) == "v" ~ "value_affirmation"),
    context = case_when(
      context == "hi" ~ "high_increasing",
      context == "hd" ~ "high_decreasing",
      context == "li" ~ "low_increasing")
  ) |>
  select(-q_num, -tone_style) |> 
  filter(!is.na(message_rating),
         str_trim(message_rating) != "")

# Sanity-check that we have 30 rows per respondent
nrow(panel) * 30 == nrow(panel_long)
```

# GLMnet Recipes

GLMnet requires a fully numeric, complete design matrix, and the penalty assumes all predictors are on the same scale. Every recipe built by `rec_glmnet_build()` (below) therefore follows the same rules:

- **Outcome:** `message_rating` is scored 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree) and modeled as numeric (gaussian GLMnet).
- **Controls (all recipes):** attitude items `q1`–`q6` as ordinal scores, and `context`, `style`, `tone`, `survey_version` dummy coded.
- **Constant demographics (all recipes):** `dem_sex` (±0.5), `dem_race` (±0.5), `dem_orientation` (dummy coded), `dem_n_household` (raw numeric).
- **Nominal features** are dummy coded with `step_dummy()` (ordered factors are first converted with `step_unorder()` so they get treatment rather than polynomial contrasts). **Ordinal features** are converted to integer scores with `step_ordinalscore()`.
- **Interactions** are built after dummy coding and before normalization. Three-way terms include their two-way terms (`(a + b + c)^3`). When adjusted income is *added*, interactions use the income bracket. When it *replaces* income bracket, Age x Income x Education uses adjusted income, and Income x Household Size is dropped because adjusted income is already a function of household size.
- In the interaction variants, `step_nzv()` removes near-zero variance interaction columns (those containing `_x_`) using the default cutoffs (ratio of most-common to second-most-common value > 95/5 and < 10% unique values). It is limited to interaction columns so that main-effect dummies for small categories are kept. `step_zv()` then removes any remaining constant columns, and `step_normalize()` scales all predictors.

Each feature option is an argument to `rec_glmnet_build()` (first value is the default):

| Argument | Options |
|---|---|
| `age` | `"numeric"`, `"nominal"` (binned, dummy coded), `"ordinal"` (binned, scored) |
| `education` | `"ordinal"` (6 levels, scored), `"nominal"` (collapsed to 3, dummy coded) |
| `income` | `"nominal"` or `"ordinal"` income bracket, or `"adjusted"` (household-adjusted income replaces the bracket) |
| `income_adjusted` | `FALSE`, or `TRUE` to add household-adjusted income alongside the bracket |
| `interactions` | `"none"`, `"all"`, or any subset of `"age_income_education"`, `"sex_race_orientation"`, `"age_household"`, `"income_household"` |

The standard set (`glmnet_configs`) crosses these options with `interactions` set to `"none"` or `"all"`: 3 x 2 x (2 x 2 + 1) = 30 main-effect configurations, each with an all-interactions variant, for 60 recipes. Each has a short label in `glmnet_configs$config` (e.g. `agenum_eduord_incord`, `agenom_edunom_incnom_adj_int`) for naming.

Demographics are constant within respondent, so the effective sample size for demographic effects is the number of respondents (n = 424), not the number of ratings. The interaction variants with several nominal features produce many sparse columns before `step_nzv()`, and penalization will be doing much of the work there.

## GLMnet Setup

The data prep and recipe builder live in `scripts/functions_llmpanel.R` (sourced in the Setup chunk) so modeling scripts can reuse them:

- `prep_glmnet_data()` converts `panel_long` to GLMnet-ready data: the outcome is scored 1–7, the Likert items and ordinal demographics become ordered factors with the correct level order, and short level labels give readable dummy column names.
- `glmnet_controls` and `glmnet_dem_constant` list the predictors included in every recipe.
- `rec_glmnet_base()` and `rec_glmnet_build()` assemble the recipes (see Recipe Builder below).

```{r}
d_glmnet <- prep_glmnet_data(panel_long)

d_glmnet |>
  select(message_rating, all_of(glmnet_controls), all_of(glmnet_dem_constant),
         dem_age, dem_age_binned, dem_education, dem_edu_collapsed,
         dem_income, dem_income_adjusted) |>
  summarise(across(everything(), \(x) sum(is.na(x)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "n_missing") |>
  filter(n_missing > 0)
```

A helper for reviewing baked feature sets:

```{r}
review_features <- function(feat) {
  predictors <- setdiff(names(feat), c("subid", "message_rating"))
  dem <- str_subset(predictors, "^dem_")
  tibble(
    n_obs = nrow(feat),
    n_predictors = length(predictors),
    n_dem_main = sum(!str_detect(dem, "_x_")),
    n_dem_interactions = sum(str_detect(dem, "_x_")),
    n_missing = sum(is.na(feat))
  ) |>
    print()
  feat |>
    select(all_of(dem), -contains("_x_")) |>
    glimpse()
}
```

## Recipe Builder

`rec_glmnet_build()` (in `functions_llmpanel.R`) takes the prepped data as its first argument, followed by the feature options in the table above. `glmnet_feature_specs` maps each option to its variable, encoding, and interaction term. The builder was checked against hand-written versions of all 60 standard recipes and produced identical feature sets.

```{r}
glmnet_feature_specs

glmnet_configs |> count(interactions)
```

## Examples

A main-effects recipe (numeric age, ordinal education, ordinal income):

```{r}
rec_glmnet_build(d_glmnet, age = "numeric", education = "ordinal", income = "ordinal")

rec_glmnet_build(d_glmnet, age = "numeric", education = "ordinal", income = "ordinal") |>
  prep() |>
  bake(new_data = NULL) |>
  review_features()
```

An interaction recipe (binned nominal age, collapsed nominal education, nominal income plus adjusted income, all interactions):

```{r}
rec_glmnet_build(d_glmnet,
                 age = "nominal",
                 education = "nominal",
                 income = "nominal",
                 income_adjusted = TRUE,
                 interactions = "all") |>
  prep() |>
  bake(new_data = NULL) |>
  review_features()
```

Interactions can also be chosen individually, e.g. only Sex x Race x Orientation and Age x Household Size:

```{r}
rec_glmnet_build(d_glmnet,
                 age = "ordinal",
                 interactions = c("sex_race_orientation", "age_household")) |>
  prep() |>
  bake(new_data = NULL) |>
  review_features()
```

All 60 standard recipes as a named list (unprepped), e.g. for a workflow set:

```{r}
glmnet_recipes <- glmnet_configs |>
  select(-config) |>
  pmap(rec_glmnet_build, data = d_glmnet) |>
  set_names(glmnet_configs$config)

length(glmnet_recipes)
```
